data.name: WolfWars
data.detailed_description:
WolfWars is a fantasy tactical strategy card game.

It may sound a bit weird, but we took & simplified rules from many other card games and created a new concept so anyone on the planet can enjoy it.

WolfWars is not a game about trading or collecting cards, but you will be able to build or edit your decks with available cards and heroes. Each player has the same amount of cards from the beginning to the end. There is no f2p/pay2win model, you all have same chances at the start.

Before you start the game, you will need to create your deck. Deck needs to have 1 hero and 5 playing cards. You can have as many decks as you wish to have. These 5 cards are all what you have during one game. You do not sacrifice any of them.

Key Features:

  • Singleplayer (PVE)
  • Cross platform multiplayer (2-4players)
  • Simultaneous turns
  • Realtime turns
  • Co-op (1vs2, 1vs3 2vs2) (players vs players & players vs AI-bot)

reviews.review:
WolfWars is a compact fantasy strategy card game that tries to distinguish itself through simplicity and competitive equality rather than enormous card collections or complicated progression systems. Developed and published by Peter Hrdy, it revolves around building a very small deck and using that limited selection efficiently against AI or human opponents. Its most appealing principle is that players receive access to the same cards instead of having to collect increasingly powerful options. This creates a level playing field where understanding the available mechanics and anticipating an opponent can matter more than accumulated content.

Deck construction is unusually streamlined. A deck consists of a hero accompanied by five selected cards, with players able to prepare and save different configurations. Rather than dealing with a huge randomized deck, the limited selection makes every choice significant before a match even begins. Cards also remain available during play instead of simply disappearing after a single use, which changes the usual rhythm associated with card battlers. The result is a system that is easy to learn while still offering opportunities to develop combinations and strategies around a chosen hero.

The available roster is relatively modest, consisting of four heroes and sixteen playing cards. This limited pool is enough to experiment with different configurations and understand the intended tactical structure, but it also exposes one of the game's greatest weaknesses. There simply are not enough cards or characters to create the enormous number of strategies found in larger deckbuilding games. Once players have tested the most obvious combinations, the possibilities can begin to feel repetitive. A significantly expanded selection would have helped the small-deck concept achieve much greater strategic depth.

Battles attempt to compensate for this limited content through mechanics involving simultaneous and real-time turns. Instead of every decision becoming a straightforward reaction to an opponent's completed action, players can be encouraged to predict what the other side intends to do. This creates opportunities for bluffing, anticipation, and tactical counterplay. The approach is especially suitable for the game's equal-access philosophy because both participants can theoretically understand what options their opponent might possess.

WolfWars includes both solo and multiplayer possibilities. AI opponents provide a way to practice the mechanics without immediately entering competitive matches, while multiplayer was designed around encounters involving two to four participants. Team arrangements and asymmetric configurations, including one-versus-two, one-versus-three, and two-versus-two battles, add some welcome flexibility. These configurations are potentially more interesting than conventional one-on-one matches because they allow the small collection of cards to be approached from different tactical perspectives.

Another notable strength is the absence of a pay-to-win structure. There is no central expectation that players repeatedly purchase cards or grind for a superior collection before they can compete effectively. Everyone works with the same basic resources, meaning experience provides knowledge rather than an automatically stronger inventory. This philosophy remains one of the most attractive aspects of the game, particularly for players who enjoy competitive card mechanics but dislike monetization systems tied to card rarity and collection advantages.

Unfortunately, the game's Early Access condition significantly affects the overall experience. WolfWars originally had broader ambitions that included additional mechanics such as creature summoning, power-ups, new locations, and environmental magical events involving storms, floods, fires, earthquakes, and sandstorms. These concepts could have introduced valuable unpredictability and battlefield variety. However, the project has gone without meaningful development activity for an exceptionally long period, leaving many of those ambitions unrealized. Players should therefore judge it according to the content that actually exists rather than expecting the proposed systems to eventually transform the experience.

This incomplete development also makes the limited amount of content much harder to overlook. The basic card mechanics show potential, but there is not enough surrounding variety to sustain prolonged engagement. A minimalist deck system can provide impressive strategic depth when supported by a broad range of cards, heroes, environments, and interactions. Here, the underlying foundation exists without enough additional material to fully exploit it. What initially feels refreshingly uncomplicated can eventually become restrictive.

Visually, the game provides a functional fantasy presentation that communicates the necessary information without delivering the elaborate effects or polished interfaces associated with modern digital card games. Its modest production values are understandable for a small independent project, and readability is ultimately more important than spectacle for this type of strategy game. Nevertheless, the presentation reinforces the impression of playing an experimental project that never progressed into a thoroughly refined final product.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially established. The game does not carry an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation, and its listed platform support is centered on Windows. As a result, Steam Deck users should consider compatibility unverified. It may potentially function through Steam's compatibility environment, but this should not be confused with official support, and controller behavior, interface usability, or other issues cannot be guaranteed.

WolfWars ultimately contains several worthwhile ideas inside an experience that feels permanently caught between prototype and finished game. Its equal-access card philosophy is commendable, the five-card deck structure creates meaningful preparation decisions, and its multiplayer configurations provide some unusual possibilities. At the same time, four heroes, sixteen cards, limited presentation, unrealized planned mechanics, and the prolonged Early Access state substantially restrict its lasting appeal. There is an interesting tactical concept here, particularly for players curious about minimalist card combat, but the game never received enough expansion and refinement to fulfill its original potential.

Rating: 5/10
